set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which scale classifies skin type by its response to ultraviolet light?
opts: The Fitzpatrick scale
Correct — six types, from always burns and never tans through to never burns.
The SCORTEN score
That estimates mortality in toxic epidermal necrolysis.
The Auspitz sign
That is a physical finding in psoriasis, not a scale.
The Nikolsky sign
That is a physical finding in blistering disease, not a scale.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which finding should raise concern for deep venous thrombosis in a patient with suspected stasis dermatitis?
opts: Acute unilateral swelling or pain
Correct. Other considerations include peripheral arterial disease, vasculitis, lymphoedema and cutaneous malignancy.
Bilateral chronic hyperpigmentation
That is the expected chronic picture of stasis dermatitis itself.
Pruritus with scaling
That fits the dermatitis rather than a thrombosis.
Atrophie blanche
That is a chronic feature of stasis disease.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What underlies xerosis, and who is most affected?
opts: An autoimmune process affecting the epithelial basement membrane, occurring most often in the elderly and remitting spontaneously after five or six years
That is bullous pemphigoid.
Impaired stratum-corneum hydration promoted by ageing, low humidity, hot water, detergents, atopy and systemic disease, commonly affecting older adults especially in winter
Correct, causing tightness, pruritus, rough scale, fissuring or eczema.
Overgrowth of Malassezia in sebum-rich areas, in young men
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Chronic venous hypertension in the lower legs, in older adults
That is stasis dermatitis.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What distinguishes a plaque from a patch?
opts: A plaque is always poorly demarcated while a patch is always well demarcated
Demarcation is described separately and varies for both.
A plaque is elevated and plateau-like; a patch is flat with no elevation
Correct — both exceed one centimetre, so elevation is the discriminator.
A plaque is larger than a patch
Both are greater than one centimetre; size does not separate them.
A plaque is fluid-filled and a patch is solid
Neither is fluid-filled.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Is urushiol contact dermatitis contagious?
opts: No, but it may spread to other areas or people if urushiol is not removed from skin or clothing
Correct — the rash itself does not spread person to person; the resin does.
Yes, direct contact with the rash transmits it
The rash is not contagious.
Yes, but only during the vesicular stage
The rash is not contagious at any stage.
No, and the resin cannot be transferred once it has dried onto clothing or bedding
Transfer from clothing and fabrics is exactly how it spreads.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How is pemphigus initially treated?
opts: With ultrapotent topical steroids alone
Those are used for mild bullous pemphigoid rather than pemphigus.
With watchful observation alone, since the disease usually remits spontaneously within five to six years without treatment
Spontaneous remission over five to six years describes bullous pemphigoid.
With oral doxycycline as monotherapy
Doxycycline is an option in moderate bullous pemphigoid, not pemphigus.
Urgently, with rituximab or high-dose oral prednisone, often alongside azathioprine or mycophenolate so steroids can be tapered off
Correct. It is a life-threatening disorder, so treatment is urgent.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is direct immunofluorescence used to diagnose in this lecture?
opts: Dermatophyte infection, by showing fungal elements within the stratum corneum
That is the role of potassium hydroxide preparation.
Herpesvirus infection, by showing multinucleated giant cells in a smear
That is the Tzanck smear.
Scabies infestation, by showing the mite, its eggs or its faecal pellets
That is the mineral oil preparation.
Autoimmune blistering disease, by showing where antibody is deposited in the skin
Correct — it is what separates bullous pemphigoid from pemphigus on a biopsy.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which first-line topical agent for mild plaque psoriasis acts quickest, and what is its caution?
opts: Salicylic acid — caution with systemic absorption in children
Salicylic acid is listed second line.
Coal tar — caution with photosensitivity
Coal tar is listed second line.
Methotrexate — caution with hepatotoxicity
Methotrexate is used for moderate to severe disease rather than as a topical first line.
Calcipotriene, a vitamin D analogue — caution with nephrotoxicity
Correct, alongside emollients, topical steroids and ultraviolet B phototherapy as first line.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which formulation is generally most occlusive, and what is it the foundation of treatment for?
opts: Gels, because they dry quickly and do not trap heat
Gels are not among the formulations compared.
Ointments, and they are the foundation of treatment for many inflammatory conditions including xerosis, eczema, irritant dermatitis and diaper dermatitis
Correct — ointments are more occlusive than creams or lotions.
Lotions, used chiefly for scalp conditions
Lotions are the least occlusive of the three.
Creams, because they spread most easily over large areas and are the foundation of treatment for xerosis, eczema, irritant dermatitis and diaper dermatitis
Creams sit between ointments and lotions in occlusiveness.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which treatment is contraindicated in pregnancy for pustular psoriasis, and what is used instead?
opts: Phototherapy is contraindicated in pregnancy; acitretin is used instead
The contraindication given is for acitretin.
Biologics are first line in pregnancy
That is not what the lecture specifies.
Acitretin is contraindicated; high-potency topical steroids are used if pregnant
Correct.
Methotrexate is safe in pregnancy and is preferred
Methotrexate is not the safe option in pregnancy.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How is mild perioral dermatitis treated once the corticosteroid is stopped?
opts: Topical ketoconazole
Antifungals are the mainstay of seborrhoeic dermatitis rather than this.
Oral prednisone
Systemic steroids are not the treatment described.
Topical metronidazole, erythromycin, pimecrolimus or azelaic acid
Correct, with oral tetracycline or doxycycline for more extensive or persistent disease.
A higher-potency topical corticosteroid applied twice daily
Continued corticosteroid exposure perpetuates the condition.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: What does this lecture say about a patient presenting with purpura?
opts: It is a benign finding common in the elderly
The lecture treats it as an emergency until disproven.
It requires only outpatient dermatology follow-up
That understates the urgency stated.
It is diagnostic of thrombocytopenia
It raises concern but is not diagnostic of any single cause.
It is a medical emergency until proven otherwise
Correct — the lecture flags it explicitly rather than treating it as one finding among many.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: How is a macule defined in this lecture?
opts: An elevated solid lesion less than one centimetre
That is a papule.
A flat elevated plateau lesion measuring greater than one centimetre across
That is a plaque.
A flat lesion less than one centimetre, without elevation or depression
Correct. A patch is the same lesion larger than one centimetre.
A flat lesion less than five millimetres
Five millimetres is the Clinical Pathophysiology convention; this course uses one centimetre.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the mechanism of alopecia areata, and why is the hair loss non-permanent?
opts: Repeated traction pulls the follicle from the scalp
That is traction alopecia, not described here.
Autoreactive T cells infiltrate the follicle and switch it from growing to resting, without destroying the stem cell compartment
Correct — the stem cells survive, so regrowth remains possible.
Autoantibodies destroy the hair follicle and its entire stem cell compartment, so that any regrowth is never possible
The stem cell compartment is preserved.
Dihydrotestosterone progressively miniaturises the follicle
That is androgenetic alopecia.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does the timing of irritant contact dermatitis vary with the irritant?
opts: All irritants produce symptoms 48 to 72 hours after exposure regardless of whether the agent is a mild soap or a concentrated acid
That timing belongs to delayed hypersensitivity in the allergic form.
Timing does not vary with the irritant
The lecture states it varies by exposure.
Mild irritants such as soaps may progress over weeks, while alkalis and acids may present within minutes or be delayed up to 24 hours or more
Correct — the agent determines the tempo.
All irritants produce symptoms within minutes of exposure
Mild irritants can take weeks.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What are the four Ps of lichen planus?
opts: Purple, painless, peripheral pustular lesions
That is not the mnemonic.
Pruritic, purple, polygonal, papules or plaques
Correct — flat-topped, pink to violaceous and shiny, coalescing into larger plaques.
Painful, pale, punched-out papules
That is not the mnemonic.
Pruritic, pustular, patchy plaques
That is not the mnemonic.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the main differential for nummular eczema, and what distinguishes them?
opts: Tinea corporis — tinea has central clearing and nummular eczema does not
Correct, and this single feature is the discriminator the lecture gives.
Psoriasis — psoriasis has silvery scale and nummular eczema does not
Psoriasis is a differential for other conditions but is not the one named here.
Pityriasis rosea — pityriasis has a herald patch
Pityriasis rosea is not the named main differential.
Contact dermatitis — contact dermatitis is well demarcated
Contact dermatitis is not the named main differential.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How is atopic dermatitis diagnosed?
opts: By skin biopsy in every case
Biopsy is reserved for atypical or refractory disease.
By serum immunoglobulin E level, which is measured routinely in every patient and establishes the diagnosis on its own without any clinical assessment
Immunoglobulin E supports the diagnosis but is not routinely tested.
By patch testing in every case
Patch testing is reserved for atypical, adult-onset or treatment-resistant disease.
Clinically, supported by family history, personal atopy, recurrent rash and elevated immunoglobulin E, though routine laboratory testing is not required
Correct. Patch testing is reserved for atypical, adult-onset or treatment-resistant disease, and biopsy for atypical or refractory disease.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Where is minoxidil primarily effective?
opts: Only in women
It is used in male-pattern hair loss, and its stated effect is at the crown.
In the crown region of the scalp
Correct — it prevents further loss and may produce regrowth, working best with finasteride.
At the frontal hairline
Its effect is primarily at the crown.
Over the entire scalp equally
Its effect is regional.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What does light microscopy show in bullous pemphigoid?
opts: Band-like infiltration of neutrophils throughout the papillary dermis
That is lichen planus.
Budding yeast and pseudohyphae
That indicates candidal infection.
Neutrophils aligned in a straight narrow row at the dermal-epidermal junction
Correct. Biopsy of a lesion goes for histopathology and perilesional tissue for direct immunofluorescence.
Acantholysis
Acantholysis is the pemphigus finding.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the mechanism of pemphigus?
opts: Autoimmune damage to the epithelial basement membrane producing subepithelial blistering that resolves without any scarring
That is bullous pemphigoid.
A type IV delayed hypersensitivity reaction to an external allergen
That is allergic contact dermatitis.
Impaired stratum-corneum hydration
That is xerosis.
Loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion, called acantholysis, from autoantibodies to adhesion molecules, producing intraepithelial blisters
Correct — a life-threatening blistering disorder of skin and mucous membranes.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What is the cornerstone of management for stasis dermatitis, and what must be established first?
opts: Compression therapy, once adequate arterial circulation has been established
Correct — an ankle-brachial index or toe pressure is considered when arterial status must be clarified before substantial compression.
Compression therapy, applied immediately in all patients on presentation
Arterial status must be established first; compression on an ischaemic limb is harmful.
Long-term systemic antibiotics
It is not an infection.
High-potency topical corticosteroids as monotherapy
A short steroid course controls inflammation but is not the cornerstone.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How does eczema change in appearance from acute to chronic?
opts: Acute shows erythema, oedema, papules, vesicles, oozing and crusting; chronic shows xerosis, fissuring, lichenification and pigment alteration
Correct, with a subacute stage of scaling, erythema, papules and excoriations between them.
Acute disease shows lichenification and pigment alteration; chronic disease shows erythema, oedema, vesicles, oozing and crusting
The stages are reversed.
The appearance is fixed and does not evolve over time
Eczema changes appearance over time, which is the point being made.
Acute shows pigment loss; chronic shows vesiculation
Neither is correct for the stage described.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which statement about topical antifungals is correct?
opts: They are effective for scalp and nail infections without any need for systemic therapy, and are the mainstay of treatment for allergic contact dermatitis
Topical therapy is explicitly inadequate for most of those.
They are ineffective against dermatophytes
They are particularly effective against them.
They are first-line for allergic contact dermatitis
That condition is not fungal.
They are particularly effective against dermatophytes, but topical therapy is inadequate for most scalp or nail infections
Correct — terbinafine, clotrimazole and ketoconazole are the agents named.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Which four features separate pemphigus from bullous pemphigoid?
opts: Subepithelial rather than intraepithelial, flaccid rather than tense blisters, a positive Nikolsky sign, and no acantholysis on biopsy
The depth and biopsy findings are wrong for pemphigus.
Intraepithelial rather than subepithelial, flaccid rather than tense blisters, positive rather than negative Nikolsky sign, and acantholysis on biopsy
Correct — the comparison table is the highest-yield slide in this section.
Subepithelial, tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign and acantholysis
That mixes the two: those are the pemphigoid features apart from acantholysis.
Intraepithelial, tense blisters, negative Nikolsky sign and no acantholysis
Tense blisters and a negative Nikolsky sign belong to pemphigoid.

set1.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set1.q: How is a poorly demarcated lesion described?
opts: Irregular or blotchy in appearance, without well-defined borders
Correct — as against a well demarcated lesion, which has clearly defined borders.
Smaller than one centimetre in every dimension measured
Demarcation is about border definition rather than size.
Present in more than one body region
That is distribution.
Raised above the surrounding skin surface
That is elevation, part of primary morphology.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: What does biopsy show in lichen planus?
opts: Band-like infiltration of lymphocytes in the dermis
Correct, with hyperkeratosis without parakeratosis, basal layer vacuolisation, Civatte bodies and a saw-tooth rete ridge.
Acantholysis
That is pemphigus.
Neutrophils in a row at the dermal-epidermal junction
That is bullous pemphigoid.
Budding yeast and pseudohyphae
That indicates candidal infection.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: How do seborrhoeic dermatitis lesions appear, and where?
opts: Coin-shaped plaques without central clearing on the extremities
That describes nummular eczema.
Tense bullae on the trunk and flexures
That describes bullous pemphigoid.
Poorly demarcated pruritic erythematous plaques 5 to 20 mm, greasy with flaking or yellow scaling, in areas rich in sebaceous glands
Correct — scalp, eyebrows, under facial hair, nasolabial creases, forehead, nose, behind the ears and the external auditory canal.
Well-demarcated salmon plaques with prominent silvery scale on the extensor elbows, knees, trunk, scalp, umbilicus and sacrum
That describes plaque psoriasis.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Why does the medication history ask when each drug was started in relation to the rash?
opts: Because only prescription medications can cause eruptions
Antibiotics, pain relievers, supplements, vitamins and herbal products are all asked about.
Because the dose determines whether a reaction is possible
Timing rather than dose is what the history targets.
Because the timing between starting a drug and the eruption is what implicates it
Correct — a new rash after starting a medication, especially with fever or mucosal sores, is an urgent warning sign.
Because most drug eruptions occur only after six months of continuous therapy
No such interval is given.

set1.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set1.q: Where does dyshidrotic eczema occur, and what are its vesicles classically called?
opts: On the scalp, with vesicles described as exclamation point lesions
Exclamation point hairs belong to alopecia areata.
On the palms, lateral and dorsal fingers and soles, with intensely pruritic vesicles described as tapioca vesicles
Correct. Vesicles may coalesce into bullae, then desiccate and resolve with desquamation.
On the flexural surfaces of the elbows and knees, with vesicles described as herald patches preceding the wider eruption
The herald patch belongs to pityriasis rosea.
On the extensor surfaces, with vesicles described as tense bullae
Tense bullae belong to bullous pemphigoid.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Where do pemphigus vulgaris lesions typically begin, and in which populations is it more common?
opts: On the scalp, and it is more common in children
Pemphigus is a disease of adults and begins in the mouth.
In the axillae, and it is endemic in rural Brazil
Endemic rural Brazil describes pemphigus foliaceus.
In the mouth, and it is more common in Jewish populations and people of Mediterranean descent
Correct. Pemphigus foliaceus by contrast is endemic in rural Brazil and rarely involves mucosa.
On the lower legs in the gaiter region, and it is far more common in older men than women
That distribution fits stasis dermatitis.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which three agents make up the medium to high potency tier?
opts: Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, hydrocortisone 1% and clobetasol propionate 0.05%
Hydrocortisone is mild and clobetasol is high.
Betamethasone valerate 0.025%, tazarotene 0.1% and adapalene 0.1% preparations
The last two are retinoids rather than corticosteroids.
Triamcinolone acetonide 0.1%, betamethasone valerate 0.1% and betamethasone dipropionate 0.05%
Correct. Betamethasone appears twice here, in two different salts.
Hydrocortisone 2.5%, betamethasone valerate 0.025% and clobetasol propionate 0.05%
Those are the mild, moderate and high agents respectively.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the atopic triad, and what proportion of patients have at least one of its components?
opts: Eczema, psoriasis and seborrhoeic dermatitis — approximately 30%
These are separate conditions rather than a triad.
Asthma, allergic rhinitis and chronic sinusitis — approximately 60%
Atopic dermatitis is part of the triad by definition.
Atopic dermatitis, asthma and allergic rhinitis — approximately 80%
Correct.
Atopic dermatitis, urticaria and food allergy — approximately 50%
Urticaria and food allergy are not the named triad.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What causes irritant contact dermatitis, and how common is it relative to the allergic form?
opts: Overgrowth of Malassezia, and it is the most common form
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
A response to chemicals or friction that disrupts the skin barrier, and it is the most common form of contact dermatitis
Correct — frequently occupational, as in healthcare and janitorial staff who wash their hands often.
A delayed type IV hypersensitivity reaction, and it is the less common form
That describes allergic contact dermatitis.
An immunoglobulin E-mediated immediate hypersensitivity reaction, and it is the most common form of contact dermatitis
Irritant contact dermatitis is not immunologically mediated.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: How are petechiae and purpura distinguished by size in this lecture?
opts: Both are defined as deposits of blood greater than 1 cm
Neither is defined that way; over 1 cm would be an ecchymosis.
Petechiae are deposits of blood 1 to 2 mm; purpura are 4 mm or greater
Correct, and purpura is flagged as a medical emergency until proven otherwise.
Petechiae are under 3 mm and purpura are 3 mm to 1 cm
That is the Clinical Pathophysiology convention rather than this lecture's.
Petechiae are 4 mm or greater and purpura are 1 to 2 mm, the reverse of the usual
The sizes are reversed.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: What defines a wheal?
opts: A deposit of blood in the skin measuring one to two millimetres across
That is a petechia.
A firm oedematous plaque produced by infiltration of fluid into the dermis
Correct — the fluid is in the tissue rather than in a cavity, which is what separates it from a vesicle.
A fluid-filled lesion containing leukocytes
That is a pustule.
A fluid-filled lesion under one centimetre
That is a vesicle.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which androgen is chiefly responsible for male-pattern hair loss?
opts: Testosterone acting directly on the follicle
Dihydrotestosterone is the androgen named.
Oestradiol
This is not the androgen responsible.
Cortisol
This is not implicated in androgenetic alopecia.
Dihydrotestosterone
Correct — male-pattern hair loss is an androgen-dependent trait with a strong paternal influence on risk.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the recommended bathing and moisturising routine for xerosis?
opts: Long hot showers taken twice daily, followed by a light fragrance-free lotion applied only once the skin has completely dried
Hot water is among the causes of xerosis.
Twice-daily antibacterial soap over the whole body
Detergents contribute to the problem.
Avoiding bathing altogether until the skin recovers
The recommendation is short lukewarm bathing followed by prompt moisturising.
Short lukewarm showers with a gentle fragrance-free cleanser only where needed, then a thick ointment or cream within minutes of bathing
Correct. Petrolatum, ceramides and humectants such as urea or lactic acid help, though keratolytics may sting fissured skin.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which patients with lichen planus are at increased risk of squamous cell carcinoma?
opts: Those with genital and erosive oral disease
Correct — an important reason to identify and follow mucosal involvement.
Those with cutaneous disease of the wrists and ankles only
The increased risk is stated for genital and erosive oral disease.
Those with nail involvement
Nail involvement occurs but is not the stated risk.
Those with hepatitis C
Hepatitis C may associate with incidence, but the malignancy risk is stated for genital and erosive oral disease.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How does the distribution of atopic dermatitis change with age?
opts: Infants: flexures and popliteal fossae. Children: extensor surfaces and scalp. Adults: cheeks, scalp and the extensor surfaces of the limbs
The infantile and childhood patterns are reversed.
The distribution is the same at every age
Distribution evolves with age, which the lecture stresses.
Infants: palms and soles. Children: trunk. Adults: lower legs
None of these matches the described pattern.
Infants: cheeks, scalp and extensor surfaces. Children: antecubital and popliteal fossae, wrists and ankles. Adults: flexures, hands, neck, face and eyelids
Correct — the shift from extensor to flexural is the pattern to hold.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What pattern does the pityriasis rosea eruption follow, and over what course?
opts: It follows a dermatome and resolves within two weeks
That describes shingles.
It follows flexural creases and persists for months
That is not the described pattern.
It appears on the extensor surfaces of the limbs and persists indefinitely unless it is treated with phototherapy
That is closer to psoriasis.
It follows cleavage lines on the trunk in a Christmas tree pattern, spreading top down over days and fading over 4 to 6 weeks
Correct. The herald patch clears centrally leaving a cigarette-paper or collarette of scale.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which supplement must accompany methotrexate?
opts: Iron
That is not the supplement given with methotrexate.
Folic acid
Correct — supplementation is given with methotrexate in every case.
Vitamin B12
That is not the supplement given with methotrexate.
Vitamin D
That is not the supplement given with methotrexate.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which finding is listed as an urgent warning sign in a patient with a rash?
opts: Fever with a rapidly spreading, painful, blistering, purple or non-blanching rash
Correct, alongside airway swelling, skin peeling involving eyes, mouth or genitals, severe pain with pus or red streaking, and a new rash after starting a medication.
Pruritus that disturbs sleep
This affects quality of life but is not on the urgent list.
A rash that has been present for more than six weeks
Chronicity alone is not an urgent warning sign.
A rash that improves steadily with over-the-counter emollients used alone twice daily
Improvement is reassuring rather than alarming.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: A fluid-filled lesion greater than one centimetre is called what?
opts: A nodule
A nodule is solid rather than fluid-filled.
A bulla
Correct — a vesicle is the same lesion up to one centimetre.
A vesicle
A vesicle is up to one centimetre.
A pustule
A pustule is defined by its leukocyte content.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What produces lichen simplex chronicus?
opts: Autoantibodies to adhesion molecules
That is pemphigus.
Overgrowth of Malassezia
That is seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Repeated rubbing and scratching triggered by itch, stress, neuropathic sensation or another dermatosis
Correct — producing intensely pruritic, well-demarcated lichenified plaques with exaggerated skin markings.
An autoimmune attack that destroys both the hair follicle and its stem cell compartment
That is alopecia areata.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which biopsy takes the whole lesion with deep and wide margins?
opts: Punch biopsy
A punch biopsy samples deeply but does not take the whole lesion with margins.
Shave biopsy
A shave biopsy removes only surface skin.
Incisional biopsy
This is not one of the three described in the lecture.
Excisional biopsy
Correct, and it always needs stitches to close.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What organism is implicated in seborrhoeic dermatitis, and who is most affected?
opts: Infection with Staphylococcus aureus, most common in children
That organism causes bacterial skin infections rather than this.
Reactivation of varicella zoster virus, most common in the elderly
That is shingles.
Overgrowth of Malassezia, most common in males aged 20 to 50
Correct — Malassezia is normal skin flora that overgrows in sebum-rich areas.
Overgrowth of Candida, most common in infants
Candida is the commonest infectious complication of diaper dermatitis instead.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which feature distinguishes irritant from candidal diaper dermatitis?
opts: Only candidal disease causes erythema
Both cause erythema; distribution is what separates them.
Irritant disease affects convex surfaces and spares the inguinal folds; candidal disease involves the folds with satellite papules or pustules
Correct — fold involvement is the discriminator, and it is called essential in the lecture.
Irritant disease involves the folds and candidal disease spares them
The pattern is reversed.
Irritant disease produces satellite papules and pustules within the inguinal folds while candidal disease spares them entirely
Satellite lesions belong to candidal disease.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What are the two primary clinical priorities in stasis dermatitis?
opts: Distinguishing it from cellulitis, and determining whether compression therapy can be used safely
Correct — both are named as the priorities.
Identifying the causative organism by culture and selecting an appropriate antibiotic
It is not an infectious condition.
Determining the allergen and arranging patch testing
That belongs to allergic contact dermatitis.
Staging the ulcer and measuring its depth
Ulceration is a complication rather than the stated priority.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which finding is pathognomonic for alopecia areata?
opts: Receding frontotemporal hairline
That is male-pattern hair loss.
Exclamation point hairs
Correct — thinner at the root and normal calibre at the top, because growth is changing in real time.
Broken hairs close to the scalp with scaling
That is tinea capitis.
Diffuse thinning of the central scalp
That is female-pattern hair loss.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which topical corticosteroid should be chosen for a sensitive site such as the face or the genitals?
opts: Clobetasol propionate, for a shorter course
A high potency agent on thin skin risks atrophy.
Betamethasone dipropionate, at half strength
That agent sits in the medium to high tier.
Triamcinolone acetonide, applied once daily
That agent sits in the medium to high tier.
Hydrocortisone, or another low potency agent
Correct — potency is selected according to site as well as severity.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: When should herpes simplex virus polymerase chain reaction be ordered in atopic dermatitis?
opts: For painful monomorphic erosions or systemic illness
Correct. Culture is reserved instead for purulent, pustular or significantly crusted lesions.
For every flare, since secondary infection is common
It is targeted to that specific presentation rather than routine.
Only when the patient has known herpes simplex
The test is used to establish it, not confirm a known case.
Only in adult-onset disease
The trigger is the lesion morphology, not the age of onset.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which agents are used for sensitive areas such as the face and eyelids in atopic dermatitis?
opts: High-potency topical corticosteroids applied to the face
High potency at those sites risks atrophy; low potency or non-steroids are preferred.
Topical retinoids
Retinoids are used for acne, photoaging and psoriasis rather than atopic dermatitis.
Topical antifungals
Atopic dermatitis is not a fungal condition.
Tacrolimus and pimecrolimus, which are calcineurin inhibitors
Correct — they avoid the atrophy risk of steroids at those sites. Crisaborole, a topical phosphodiesterase-4 inhibitor, is also used.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How can atopic dermatitis appear differently across skin tones?
opts: Identical on all skin tones, since the eruption is defined by its distribution
Distribution helps, but the appearance genuinely differs.
Violaceous on lighter skin, but hypopigmented on darker skin in every case
That is not how the difference is described.
Angry and inflamed on lighter skin, but almost silvery on darker skin
Correct — the underlying disease is the same but the visual signal is not.
Silvery on lighter skin, but angry and inflamed on darker skin
That reverses the two descriptions.

set2.io: Objective a — Anatomy of the integumentary system
set2.q: Which six features are used to translate a dermatological finding into words?
opts: Onset, duration, severity, triggers, treatments tried and response
Those come from the history rather than the description of the lesion.
Location, laterality, symmetry, tenderness, temperature and texture
These are not the six features named.
Primary morphology, secondary morphology, demarcation, colour, size and distribution
Correct. Getting all six into a description is what lets another provider picture the lesion without seeing it.
Primary morphology, colour and distribution only, since the rest are subjective
Demarcation, secondary morphology and size are all part of the description.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: What is the Auspitz sign?
opts: Fine white lines on the surface of a plaque
Those are Wickham's striae.
Removal of scale produces bleeding
Correct — a classic psoriasis finding, alongside Koebner's phenomenon.
Lesions appear at sites of trauma
That is the Koebner phenomenon.
The top layers of skin slough when rubbed
That is the Nikolsky sign.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: How is pityriasis rosea treated?
opts: It is self-limited, so reassurance is the mainstay, with antihistamines or topical steroids used cautiously for pruritus
Correct. Ultraviolet B phototherapy or sunlight helps if begun in the first week; severe cases may be treated with acyclovir.
A tapering course of oral prednisone given over a period of two to three weeks from the outset of the eruption
That is used for severe allergic contact dermatitis.
Topical ketoconazole
That treats seborrhoeic dermatitis.
Oral doxycycline for six weeks
That is not the treatment for this condition.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Who most commonly develops nummular eczema?
opts: Men, and more often adults over the age of 50, though it can occur at any age
Correct. It is likely caused by some degree of skin barrier dysfunction.
Women in their twenties and thirties
It is more common in men and in older adults.
Infants and young children
That pattern fits atopic dermatitis rather than nummular eczema.
Adolescents in the weeks following a streptococcal throat infection
That pattern fits guttate psoriasis.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, manifestations, differential diagnosis, testing, management, referrals, education and prognosis of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which examination approach is most reliable when erythema is difficult to appreciate on darker skin?
opts: Palpation for warmth and oedema, with attention to distribution and secondary change
Correct — colour stops being the primary signal, so the other findings carry the diagnosis.
Wood's lamp examination of every affected area in a darkened room
That is used for selected fungal and bacterial infections and for pigment change.
Immediate skin biopsy of the affected area, since clinical diagnosis is unreliable
Most of these conditions remain clinical diagnoses.
Potassium hydroxide preparation from the affected area in every patient
That test addresses fungal infection specifically.

set2.io: Objective c — Etiologies, manifestations, diagnosis and management of dermatological conditions
set2.q: Which barrier protein is most notably reduced in atopic dermatitis?
opts: Filaggrin
Correct — reduced filaggrin production is the named epidermal-barrier defect, alongside immune dysregulation.
Keratin
Keratin is the structural protein of the epidermis but is not the named defect here.
Collagen
Collagen is a dermal protein and is not implicated in this way.
Elastin
Elastin provides recoil and is not the barrier protein named.
